answer: History, not a forecast. From late 1997 to Aug 2026 funeral prices rose 3.31% a year, faster than prices overall (2.58%) and faster than rolling 3-month T-bills paid (2.15%). Money set aside in T-bills instead of prepaying fell short of the same funeral 10 years later in 91.5% of start months (224 starts, Dec 1997 to Aug 2016); the median 10-year saver could pay 83.9% of the funeral (range 75.2% to 108.4%), and the latest 10-year saver (Aug 2016 to Aug 2026) 80.3%. Over 5 years the savings fell short in 88.7% of starts, over 15 years in 100%. T-bills paid 3.72% in Aug 2026.
guess: Common advice treats a prepaid funeral as a poor deal: most retirees would guess that keeping the money in safe interest-bearing savings keeps up with funeral prices, so locking today's price buys nothing but convenience.
changesDecision: Over the whole period with a funeral price index, safe savings almost never kept pace with funeral prices; a fully price-guaranteed plan would have locked in a real advantage in roughly nine of ten starts. That reframes the choice: the price question has historically favored locking, so the decision turns on the contract risks (what is guaranteed, cancellation, portability, provider failure) rather than on returns. No forecast of prices or rates is made.

assumptions: The prepaid plan is fully price-guaranteed for the covered goods and services: the family pays nothing more at the time of need, whatever prices have done.
The national funeral expenses index stands in for the price of one specific funeral; local prices and individual choices differ.

The alternative keeps exactly the prepaid amount in 3-month T-bills, rolled monthly at the monthly average rate divided by 12; the bill rate is the discount-basis quote, not converted to an investment yield.
Taxes on T-bill interest, trust or insurance fees inside prepaid plans, installment-plan finance charges, cancellation refunds and provider failure are all ignored.
Cash-advance items that funeral homes pass through (cemetery fees, death certificates, obituaries) are usually not guaranteed and are not separated in the index.
limits: History, not a forecast. The funeral price index starts in Dec 1997, so every window sits in a period of mostly low short-term rates; overlapping windows give only about three independent 10-year periods. Ignoring taxes favors the T-bill side. The result says nothing about whether a particular contract is guaranteed, portable or refundable.
